500DqeTR15g.title: Ramadan 2025 Night 15: Quranic Themes, Honouring Parents
500DqeTR15g.one_line: Birr al-walidayn rightly understood: not a tool of control, but the barakah of righteous parents, Ibrahim's gentle words to his father, and a mother's love for Musa.
500DqeTR15g.summary: He notes that honouring parents, once a topic everyone nodded along to, now brings red faces, while dishonouring parents is among the signs of the Hour. He warns against using Quranic verses on others when your own interest is involved: read them about yourself, and keep honouring parents after they die by representing them well and caring for siblings, as Yusuf spared his brothers for his parents' sake. Birr does not give parents control over a child's studies, appearance or choice of spouse beyond advising and objecting to real ethical or religious problems; the parent's right is to have their needs met, and overplaying the birr card ruins its sanctity. From 18:82 he explains that Al-Khidr rebuilt the wall to protect two orphans' treasure because their father was righteous, so many unseen blessings in your life may come from your parents' barakah. From 19:41-48 he shows Ibrahim speaking to a hostile father with affection, logic and humility, attributing his insight to knowledge received rather than superiority, and answering threats with peace; children are not tasked with fixing their parents. From 20:37-40 and 28:10 he describes Musa's mother's grief, and ends with the Prophet's answer: your mother, your mother, your mother, then your father.

outline.heading: A famous theme that now stirs emotion
outline.gist: Honouring parents is a hallmark of the faith, and talking about it used to bring easy agreement and sentiment.

outline.heading: From nods to red faces
outline.gist: Over the past decade he has seen disagreement, while some parents ask him to repeat it to their children.

outline.heading: A sign of the Hour
outline.gist: Scholars read the slave woman giving birth to her own master as the mistreatment of parents, among the signs that the Hour is near.

outline.heading: Never use the Quran on others for your own interest
outline.gist: Parents should be careful wielding these verses on their children; read them as commands for yourself, at any age.

outline.heading: Honouring parents after they die
outline.gist: You represent them on earth, and caring for the siblings and family they loved honours them; cutting off a sibling dishonours them.

outline.heading: Yusuf spared his brothers for his parents
outline.gist: He did not punish his brothers partly so his father and mother would not suffer a torn family.

outline.heading: Birr is not control over marriage
outline.gist: Parents may advise on a spouse and push back on real ethical or religious problems, but the choice remains the child's.

outline.heading: The parent's right is support, not your life choices
outline.gist: Culture, income or a course of study are not grounds for invoking birr; the duty is to meet parents' financial, social and emotional needs.

outline.heading: Overplaying the birr card
outline.gist: He often cannot side with parents who demand the ridiculous; overusing a sacred concept, like calling everything haram, empties it of meaning.

outline.heading: The midpoint of Ramadan
outline.gist: The first half welcomes the month and the second bids it farewell, so cherish this last night of welcoming it.

outline.heading: Al-Khidr as a symbol of Allah's decree
outline.gist: His actions represent knowledge we cannot learn from or imitate, such as why a child's life is taken.

outline.heading: The stingy village and the wall
outline.gist: Refused food and water, Al-Khidr rebuilt their collapsing wall for free, and Musa objected.

outline.heading: Decree cannot always be reasoned out
outline.gist: Musa tried to understand logically, so they parted; some say he witnessed more incidents but objected only three times.

outline.heading: The wall belonged to two orphans
outline.gist: A treasure lay beneath it, their father was righteous, and Allah wanted them to grow up and take it themselves; none of it was his own decision.

outline.heading: Why rebuilding protected the treasure
outline.gist: Had the wall fallen soon, the village's untrustworthy people would have controlled the young orphans' wealth.

outline.heading: We know almost nothing
outline.gist: Our sliver of knowledge cannot show what is best; we plan, do our best and trust the One who knows all.

outline.heading: The barakah of righteous parents
outline.gist: Allah's command to honour parents reflects that you live through the barakah of their hard work.

outline.heading: Even parents who are not Muslim
outline.gist: Many companions had non-Muslim parents, yet the good their parents did could still benefit them, unearned.

outline.heading: Why the father is mentioned
outline.gist: The verse would make sense without the phrase, but Allah names the reason: you do not know what good reached you, or what harm was held back, because of your parents.

outline.heading: The boys never knew
outline.gist: They likely found the treasure and lived well without knowing it was their father's goodness, as we often do.

outline.heading: Ibrahim's longest talk with his father
outline.gist: The most detailed account of their conversation; Ibrahim was heartbroken that his father would not join him and instead cursed and threatened him.

outline.heading: Ya abati: the language of affection
outline.gist: Ibrahim used an endearing form of 'my father' to soften his heart, the kind of pet name children use with parents.

outline.heading: A logical question and knowledge received
outline.gist: He asked why worship what neither hears nor sees, then said it was not his father's fault, he had simply received knowledge.

outline.heading: Do not follow Shaytan; I fear for you
outline.gist: He warned against following one who does not love him, used the name Ar-Rahman, and voiced fear for his father.

outline.heading: It is not your job to fix your parents
outline.gist: Parents rarely change because their children tell them to; your role is to honour, help and protect them.

outline.heading: Only knowledge tips the scales
outline.gist: Ibrahim spoke because revelation gave him something his father lacked; if you truly outlearn your parents it will show in how you live.

outline.heading: The arrogance of lecturing parents
outline.gist: Objecting because your culture differs from theirs, or claiming to have figured it all out, lacks adab; Ibrahim asked, explained, showed care and expressed fear.

outline.heading: His father's threat
outline.gist: His father threatened to stone him and disowned him.

outline.heading: Peace be upon you
outline.gist: Ibrahim answered with peace and a promise to ask forgiveness for him, which he was later told to stop.

outline.heading: Respect for a father who opposed him
outline.gist: Though his father helped throw him into the fire, Ibrahim stayed respectful, as the Prophet pleaded with Abu Talib; losing a loved one outside Islam is a unique pain.

outline.heading: Musa's fear before Pharaoh
outline.gist: When Musa grew anxious about his mission, Allah reminded him of what He revealed to his mother.

outline.heading: Casting her baby into the Nile
outline.gist: A mother placed her child in a chest on the river toward an enemy; Allah cast His love on Musa so he would be raised under His eye.

outline.heading: His sister and the return to his mother
outline.gist: His sister offered Pharaoh's household a nurse, and Musa was returned so his mother's eye would be cooled.

outline.heading: Her heart became empty
outline.gist: Narrations describe her staring into nothing, unable to hear, see or eat, such is a parent's love.

outline.heading: You understand your parents once you are one
outline.gist: Raising your own child shows how hard it is to hold a family together, and changes how you see your parents.

outline.heading: Your mother, your mother, your mother
outline.gist: They gave you their best years, so you owe them some of yours, not weeks without care while you are strong.

41:34.ar: وَلَا تَسۡتَوِي ٱلۡحَسَنَةُ وَلَا ٱلسَّيِّئَةُۚ ٱدۡفَعۡ بِٱلَّتِي هِيَ أَحۡسَنُ فَإِذَا ٱلَّذِي بَيۡنَكَ وَبَيۡنَهُۥ عَدَٰوَةࣱ كَأَنَّهُۥ وَلِيٌّ حَمِيمࣱ‏

Fcm5NRYRvE4.speaker_note: continues his own Tazkiyah Pearls series and tells a Damascene story from his upbringing
Fcm5NRYRvE4.title: Tazkiyah Pearls 6: The Soul, the Cycle and the Qalb (Subconscious)
Fcm5NRYRvE4.one_line: How the nafs works and is tamed, the conscience, the thought-action-feeling cycle, and changing feelings by changing what enters the heart.
Fcm5NRYRvE4.summary: He deepens the picture of the nafs: made from the earth, it is programmed for survival and superiority, indifferent to whether means are lawful, unaware of what is truly good for you, unwilling to act unless there is something in it for itself, and unable to accept delayed reward, much like a selfish toddler. Many of its convictions, such as believing you deserve good things, should be kept but rewired to the right source; those whose nafs lost that belief through abuse need therapy. The goal is to tame the nafs, not break it, and he describes five levels for each behaviour, from total surrender to the nafs through a seesaw, forced compliance and resigned habit, to agreement. The conscience is the ruh's influence on the nafs, and its death is the beginning of death. He then presents the cycle in which thoughts, actions and feelings shape one another: we control our actions fully, our thoughts partly through reflection, and our feelings not at all. A Damascene story of a woman who set out to poison her mother-in-law with nightly massages shows good actions changing hatred into love. Feelings come from the heart's mixing pot of what we see, hear, think and are surrounded by, so he asks listeners to change their inputs and expectations patiently, since tazkiyah is slow.

outline.heading: Opening
The nafs is programmed for survival
outline.gist: Coming from the soil of the earth, the nafs, like all life, wants to survive, dominate and take in the most energy for the least effort.

outline.heading: It cares about outcomes, not means
outline.gist: Halal or haram means nothing to it; it loves you but does not know what is best, which is why domesticated animals and people overeat.

outline.heading: There must be something in it for the nafs
outline.gist: Selflessness is hard because the nafs resists anything that profits it nothing, such as strengthening someone else; it is not evil, just programmed, so we do not hate it.

outline.heading: No delayed reward: a toddler inside
outline.gist: A bird in the hand beats ten in the tree; the nafs trusts no one and is a selfish child we carry within.

outline.heading: Keep its convictions, change the reasons
outline.gist: Believing you deserve good things is essential and should be rewired to Allah as its source; those whose nafs lost it through abuse need real therapy.

outline.heading: Tame the nafs, do not break it
outline.gist: A broken nafs leaves a person without integrity or courage; taming happens in levels.

outline.heading: Level one: no resistance
outline.gist: Like a parent who gives a two-year-old everything, the person simply submits to whatever the nafs wants.

outline.heading: Level two: the seesaw
outline.gist: Some days you win and some days the nafs wins; your level differs for each behaviour.

outline.heading: Level three: forcing the nafs
outline.gist: The nafs hates it but has no choice, as with most people going to work or sometimes to Fajr.

outline.heading: Level four: the nafs gives up
outline.gist: It stops fighting and the act becomes habit, though without passion and with the nafs still thinking it wasteful.

outline.heading: Level five: the nafs agrees
outline.gist: As in play, the nafs wants what you want; the hope is to reach this for the deeds that bring us close to Allah.

outline.heading: The conscience: the ruh's effect on the nafs
outline.gist: The stronger the spirit's influence on the nafs, the stronger the conscience; it is one nafs with different states.

outline.heading: The death of the conscience
outline.gist: Death begins when the spirit no longer influences the nafs; a good upbringing, environment and values of compassion strengthen the spirit.

outline.heading: Connection to Allah as an endless source
outline.gist: Those good before Islam became good in Islam; without a link to Allah the spirit shrivels and needs constant upkeep.

outline.heading: The cycle of thoughts, actions and feelings
outline.gist: Each one affects and is affected by the other two, so the cycle is always virtuous or vicious.

outline.heading: How much of each we control
outline.gist: We control all our actions, a variable share of our thoughts that grows with contemplation, and none of our feelings directly.

outline.heading: Breaking a vicious cycle
outline.gist: Disliking someone breeds negative thoughts and bad actions that deepen the dislike; jam a rod in the wheel by deliberately thinking and acting well.

outline.heading: The mother-in-law and the poison lotion
outline.gist: A Damascene apothecary gave a woman plain lotion to massage her mother-in-law nightly; after twenty days she came back begging for an antidote because she now loved her.

outline.heading: Feelings are the strongest part of the cycle
outline.gist: Strong feelings power both thoughts and actions, raising the question of how to influence what we cannot control.

outline.heading: The qalb's four inputs
outline.gist: The heart mixes what we see, what we hear, our environment and our thoughts, and its output is our emotions.

outline.heading: The heart loves what it is fed, with a lag
outline.gist: Feeding it haram sights, sounds, company and thoughts makes it love haram; changes take months to show as old input filters out.

outline.heading: Turning a hated chore neutral through expectations
outline.gist: Taking out garbage or driving siblings feels awful when thought of negatively; treating it as a given makes the heart neutral about it.

outline.heading: Learning to enjoy what is not play, including salah
outline.gist: Changing outlook and associations can make a non-playful act joyful, which is how prayer moves from habit to enjoyment.

outline.heading: Tazkiyah is slow, not an aha moment
outline.gist: Few are granted a sudden transformation; most must identify their nafs and change thoughts and inputs to change behaviour over time.

outline.heading: Why everyone wants a front lawn
outline.gist: Our subconscious absorbed the background of films, so we want houses, cars and lawns without knowing why; change what you look at, listen to and surround yourself with.

outline.heading: Everything returns to this cycle
outline.gist: These simple principles let you take back control, changing how you feel about even tiring acts of worship.

9:23.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ لَا تَتَّخِذُوٓاْ ءَابَآءَكُمۡ وَإِخۡوَٰنَكُمۡ أَوۡلِيَآءَ إِنِ ٱسۡتَحَبُّواْ ٱلۡكُفۡرَ عَلَى ٱلۡإِيمَٰنِۚ وَمَن يَتَوَلَّهُم مِّنكُمۡ فَأُوْلَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلظَّٰلِمُونَ
9:23.en: O you who have believed, do not take your fathers or your brothers as allies if they have preferred disbelief over belief. And whoever does so among you - then it is those who are the wrongdoers

9:24.ar: قُلۡ إِن كَانَ ءَابَآؤُكُمۡ وَأَبۡنَآؤُكُمۡ وَإِخۡوَٰنُكُمۡ وَأَزۡوَٰجُكُمۡ وَعَشِيرَتُكُمۡ وَأَمۡوَٰلٌ ٱقۡتَرَفۡتُمُوهَا وَتِجَٰرَةࣱ تَخۡشَوۡنَ كَسَادَهَا وَمَسَٰكِنُ تَرۡضَوۡنَهَآ أَحَبَّ إِلَيۡكُم مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِۦ وَجِهَادࣲ فِي سَبِيلِهِۦ فَتَرَبَّصُواْ حَتَّىٰ يَأۡتِيَ ٱللَّهُ بِأَمۡرِهِۦۗ وَٱللَّهُ لَا يَهۡدِي ٱلۡقَوۡمَ ٱلۡفَٰسِقِينَ
9:24.en: Say, [O Muhammad], "If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your wives, your relatives, wealth which you have obtained, commerce wherein you fear decline, and dwellings with which you are pleased are more beloved to you than Allah and His Messenger and jihad in His cause, then wait until Allah executes His command. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people

2:219.ar: ۞يَسۡـَٔلُونَكَ عَنِ ٱلۡخَمۡرِ وَٱلۡمَيۡسِرِۖ قُلۡ فِيهِمَآ إِثۡمࣱ كَبِيرࣱ وَمَنَٰفِعُ لِلنَّاسِ وَإِثۡمُهُمَآ أَكۡبَرُ مِن نَّفۡعِهِمَاۗ وَيَسۡـَٔلُونَكَ مَاذَا يُنفِقُونَۖ قُلِ ٱلۡعَفۡوَۗ كَذَٰلِكَ يُبَيِّنُ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمُ ٱلۡأٓيَٰتِ لَعَلَّكُمۡ تَتَفَكَّرُونَ
2:219.en: They ask you about wine and gambling. Say, "In them is great sin and [yet, some] benefit for people. But their sin is greater than their benefit." And they ask you what they should spend. Say, "The excess [beyond needs]." Thus Allah makes clear to you the verses [of revelation] that you might give thought

9:111.ar: ۞إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ ٱشۡتَرَىٰ مِنَ ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ أَنفُسَهُمۡ وَأَمۡوَٰلَهُم بِأَنَّ لَهُمُ ٱلۡجَنَّةَۚ يُقَٰتِلُونَ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ فَيَقۡتُلُونَ وَيُقۡتَلُونَۖ وَعۡدًا عَلَيۡهِ حَقࣰّ ا فِي ٱلتَّوۡرَىٰةِ وَٱلۡإِنجِيلِ وَٱلۡقُرۡءَانِۚ وَمَنۡ أَوۡفَىٰ بِعَهۡدِهِۦ مِنَ ٱللَّهِۚ فَٱسۡتَبۡشِرُواْ بِبَيۡعِكُمُ ٱلَّذِي بَايَعۡتُم بِهِۦۚ وَذَٰلِكَ هُوَ ٱلۡفَوۡزُ ٱلۡعَظِيمُ
9:111.en: Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties [in exchange] for that they will have Paradise. They fight in the cause of Allah, so they kill and are killed. [It is] a true promise [binding] upon Him in the Torah and the Gospel and the Qur'an. And who is truer to his covenant than Allah? So rejoice in your transaction which you have contracted. And it is that which is the great attainment

vejhCEZQ1rc.speaker_note: Ramadan Quranic Themes night at MWN; refers to his own 2024 khutbahs and to people who approach him as imam
vejhCEZQ1rc.title: Ramadan 2025 Night 9: Quranic Themes, Recipes for Success
vejhCEZQ1rc.one_line: Three Quranic recipes for success: pardon and low expectations with people (7:199-200), unity without dispute (8:46), and loving Allah above all (9:23-24).
vejhCEZQ1rc.summary: He presents the Quran's recurring lists of the qualities of the successful as recipes: each passage varies slightly, so there is more than one path, and a believer should pick one passage and hold himself to it daily. The first recipe, from 7:199-200, governs dealings with people: accept whatever people can offer and keep expectations low, make pardon a way of life except in the face of oppression, which must be resisted, encourage good customs, walk away from the ignorant without arguing, and seek refuge in Allah when Shaytan stirs anger. He applies low expectations to marriage and recounts how hostile people repeatedly became friends and volunteers. The second, from 8:46, is communal: obey Allah and His Messenger and do not dispute, since disagreement is human but tanazu' means parting ways, and it brings failure and lost momentum. He points to divided Muslim communities in Canadian cities and to two billion Muslims unable to stop the massacre in Gaza, urging the young to feel urgency. The third, from 9:23-24, is of the heart: family, wealth, homes and businesses may be loved, but never more than Allah, His Prophet and striving for Him, as Abu Lahab's story shows.

outline.heading: The Quran's recurring recipes for success
outline.gist: Passages describing the people of Jannah vary slightly, and following any one set of these qualities leads to success.

outline.heading: Advice people wish they had followed
outline.gist: Successful people often recommend what they regret not doing, so weigh their advice carefully.

outline.heading: Keep the company of achievers
outline.gist: Success breeds success; reading the Quran puts you in the company of Allah and the prophets and the advice they lived by.

outline.heading: No single recipe, but common lines
outline.gist: The variation shows there is more than one way to succeed, while salah, zakah and humility recur in nearly every list.

outline.heading: Choose one passage and hold yourself to it
outline.gist: Pick at least one recipe and check every day whether you are meeting its milestones.

outline.heading: Al-Anfal as a recipe for a nation's success
outline.gist: The whole surah, with its laws of victory, describes the success of an ummah, which is why this theme suits tonight's portion.

outline.heading: Quranic themes as the canvas of the Quran
outline.gist: Any theme can be traced through any night's verses because these themes are the underlying maxims the Quran teaches throughout.

outline.heading: Take what people can give
outline.gist: Al-'afw means accepting whatever people offer; the lower your expectations, the happier, kinder and calmer you become.

outline.heading: Pardon as a way of life
outline.gist: The second meaning is to live by forgiving and not carrying grudges over others' harsh words or misjudgments.

outline.heading: No pardon while oppression continues
outline.gist: When rights or land are taken, forgiving is weakness that invites more oppression; reclaim your rights first, then forgive if you wish.

outline.heading: Two words, a whole lifestyle
outline.gist: In ordinary daily friction, when people are rude or unkind, let it go and move on.

outline.heading: Low expectations in marriage
outline.gist: Most marriages fail because both spouses expect too much; when expectations are low, every kindness becomes a bonus and happiness is the baseline.

outline.heading: Only Allah never disappoints
outline.gist: People will always disappoint you; hold high expectations only of those who ask you to mentor them.

outline.heading: Turn away from the ignorant
outline.gist: After encouraging good customs, do not argue with people who only seek your mistakes; let them finish and walk away, since most happiness is choosing your battles.

outline.heading: Answering bizarre comments with a dua
outline.gist: Faced with requests so strange he cannot begin to answer, he blesses the person and avoids the conversation next time.

outline.heading: Seek refuge when Shaytan kindles anger
outline.gist: When the urge rises to expose someone's ignorance, seek refuge in Allah, who hears and knows, from anger you will regret.

outline.heading: Hostile people who came around
outline.gist: Following this recipe, many who once despised him later became friends, congregants and volunteers; he restates its four parts.

outline.heading: A communal recipe: obey Allah and His Messenger
outline.gist: Unlike the first, personal recipe, this one concerns the ummah's success and begins with obedience.

outline.heading: Disagreement is human, dispute is not
outline.gist: Tanazu' is not differing in opinion but tearing unity apart until people refuse to work together.

outline.heading: The ummah is short on time
outline.gist: Other nations move fast toward their goals; the young must develop an urgency his generation lacked, with 75 years of occupation as the measure.

outline.heading: Failure and lost momentum
outline.gist: Disputes bring failure and make the ummah's wind stop blowing, the momentum people need to serve their community.

outline.heading: Divided Muslim communities in the West
outline.gist: Muslims in Western cities achieve little because leaders run small silos and will not sit together and plan.

outline.heading: Persevere to keep unity
outline.gist: Avoiding dispute is hard when dealing with difficult people, but Allah is with those who persevere, as the Prophet did.

outline.heading: Two billion Muslims could not stop a massacre
outline.gist: A quarter of humanity agrees on the sanctity of the holy land yet could not stop fifteen months of killing; the missing piece is unity.

outline.heading: Do not take hostile relatives as allies
outline.gist: Keep showing parents kindness whatever they do, but do not make relatives who work against your faith your closest allies.

outline.heading: The eight beloved things
outline.gist: Fathers, children, brothers, spouses, tribe, wealth, homes and businesses, if any is more beloved than Allah, His Messenger and striving for Him.

outline.heading: An explicit threat over what you love most
outline.gist: This is a matter of love in the heart, not decision-making, and unlike the Quran's many implied warnings, this threat is explicit.

outline.heading: Love them, just not more
outline.gist: All eight are things you are expected or commanded to love; the problem is comparison, not essence.

outline.heading: Passion for the deen like for a sick child
outline.gist: Nothing will change until our passion for Islam and the ummah at least matches what we feel for a sick child.

outline.heading: The ingredients must be right
outline.gist: Love for Allah must outweigh everything else combined, or one day the heavier love wins and you cannot give your life and wealth for Him.

outline.heading: Abu Lahab loved the Prophet, but not most
outline.gist: He celebrated the Prophet's birth and engaged his sons to his daughters, yet loved his wealth and status more.

outline.heading: Beware what you let yourself love
outline.gist: Love can be shaped indirectly with finesse; he recalls the three recipes for etiquette, unity and the heart.

outline.heading: Outro

BMsih8FnXaw.title: Ramadan Reminders 1446: Part 1, The Opportunity
BMsih8FnXaw.one_line: Ramadan is the greatest opportunity Allah offers, given only to those who value it; renew intentions, keep knocking and avoid distractions.
BMsih8FnXaw.summary: Around the point in Ramadan when masjid attendance always starts to dip, the sheikh offers an analogy: if you open a rare door for someone and watch them slack, you will not offer them the next opportunity, and nobody would blame you. Ramadan is Allah's opportunity, with Paradise open and your heart called to Him, and every job, scholarship or investment ranks far below it. Closeness to Allah, unlike worldly goods, is given only to those who value it and can be withdrawn when they stop, which is why many long for a connection they had when younger; it can still return with divine interest. His first reminder, repeated every year, is to revise your intention daily, since good intention covers shortcomings. Allah's commodity is expensive: as a sixteen-year-old in Syria he crossed an hour of transit to his Quran teacher, was sent home three times, and was taught only after returning a fourth time, because the teacher had to know he wanted it. Embrace the fatigue as reward. In the second khutbah he warns against small distractions, especially phones and social media, urges men to prioritise Fajr and Isha in congregation, and ends with the hadith that Allah comes faster to those who approach Him.

outline.heading: Opening
The dip in the Ramadan graph
outline.gist: Around this point every year attendance starts to fall and full masjids thin out. But Ramadan is not its first or last few days; it is a whole-month opportunity.

outline.heading: Waste an opportunity and the giver moves on
outline.gist: If you work to get someone a job or scholarship they could never get alone and watch them slack, you will quietly give the next chance to someone else, even if you did it for Allah, and nobody would blame you.

outline.heading: Ramadan: Allah's opportunity
outline.gist: Allah has the highest example. One month in twelve He opens Paradise, closes Hell and calls your heart to know and connect with Him; nothing in life comes close.

outline.heading: Every other opportunity is a distant second
outline.gist: Picture the scholarship, admission, job or investment you most want: all rank far below the chance for your heart to connect with Allah. If you do not see it that way, you will not get it.

outline.heading: Meat for someone with no teeth
outline.gist: Allah gives worldly things even to people who do not value them, as the Arabic proverb puts it. What pains him most is a gifted intellect wasted.

outline.heading: His closeness, only for those who value it
outline.gist: Drawing near to Allah is hard, and His closeness and love are given only to those who understand their worth. Stop valuing the connection and He takes it back.

outline.heading: Lost closeness can return with interest
outline.gist: Many look back on a younger self who felt close to Allah and cannot find it again. It can come back better than before, with divine interest, once you show Him it matters most.

outline.heading: Show Him this is the best offer you have had
outline.gist: Show Allah you would not trade these days of fasting and nights of prayer for anything. The two-week waterfall in attendance reveals hearts missing what He offers.

outline.heading: Reminder one: revise your intentions
outline.gist: Those who are on call or truly cannot attend still get the full reward. Ramadan is won by intention, and good intention makes up for weak action.

outline.heading: Intention carries you through stumbling
outline.gist: Keep revising daily and recall what you asked for at the start: freedom from punishment, Paradise without reckoning, being with your family, repentance and a mended heart.

outline.heading: Knock on the only door that can give it
outline.gist: If you have not received it yet, come for every prayer and keep knocking, for years if needed. No one else owns these things to give; Allah's commodity is expensive, and it is Paradise.

outline.heading: Sent home three times in Damascus
outline.gist: At 16 he left school early, waited for buses and walked uphill in his military-style uniform to reach his Quran teacher, who sent him home three times. When he wanted to quit, his father said it was not up for negotiation.

outline.heading: I needed to know you wanted it
outline.gist: On the fourth visit he was accepted, and the man is still his teacher. Asked why, the teacher said he had to see he truly wanted it; Allah's gift is no different.

outline.heading: Keep knocking, Ramadan after Ramadan
outline.gist: What Allah offers is priceless, so prove you want it. It may not come in the first, tenth or twentieth Ramadan; knocking for two days and returning on the 27th night does not work.

outline.heading: Bathe in the fatigue
outline.gist: Embrace the exhaustion: you are tired only because of fasting and night prayer, not a late show or a holiday, and every bit of it is being banked as reward.

outline.heading: Interlude
The final reminder: beware of distractions
outline.gist: Shaytan is chained but left distractions behind. The ego hates serious things, so we procrastinate with trivia; small distractions add up.

outline.heading: Phones and screens drain the month's baraka
outline.gist: Are the social media apps still on your phone? Images that are borderline or worse, and hours of worthless screen time, pull your mind from the beauty of the month.

outline.heading: Lost through small mistakes
outline.gist: People rarely lose everything through one catastrophe; a chain of small bad decisions strips time of its baraka. For men, praying in congregation must take priority.

outline.heading: The heavy, cold prayers first
outline.gist: Fajr and Isha are the heavy prayers, and showing up when it is cold is true commitment. Then pray taraweeh and push past your habits, since you are asking for what you can never deserve.

outline.heading: Fathers who watch their gifts ignored
outline.gist: Most conflict between parents and children comes from fathers who wear themselves out for opportunities their children do not value. Seeing an opportunity used makes the giver give more.

outline.heading: Show Him you are serious
outline.gist: Do not give up at the first difficulty; come back tomorrow and the day after. Whoever comes to Allah a little, He comes twice as far.

outline.heading: Outro

P1v5TEkMZ0c.title: Tafsir of Surat Al-Saffat, Part 3: Verses 28-50
P1v5TEkMZ0c.one_line: Leaders and followers blame each other in Hell, la ilaha illa Allah as the liberating truth, and the sincere servants' rewards beyond their deeds.
P1v5TEkMZ0c.summary: He frames the passage as more of the unseen: conversations on Judgment Day we could never know without revelation, set against how tiny we are in the cosmos and how humbling it is that Allah cares for us. In verses 28-32 followers accuse leaders of misleading them through power or a show of piety, and the leaders reply that the followers never believed and simply wanted their narrative. He connects this to echo chambers: social media algorithms only automate the old habit of surrounding ourselves with people who say what we want to hear. Growth needs voices that make us uncomfortable, and his own job is to challenge, not mirror. A shameless, lying leader of the country to the south is the collective mirror of what people want to hear. Both leader and follower share the punishment, as criminals against Allah's law. The rejected statement in verse 35 is la ilaha illa Allah, the simplest explanation of existence and a phrase that frees a person from fearing or obeying anyone but Allah; rejecting it takes arrogance, and modern people still effectively worship rulers. Everyone is repaid exactly for their deeds except the sincere servants, whose sincerity is granted by Allah and who receive far more than they did: food for pleasure, honour, company, a pure drink that harms neither body nor mind, and loyal spouses, with every joy free of harm.

outline.heading: Three pages of the unseen
outline.gist: The surah lists the unseen, now moving to Judgment Day conversations we would never know without revelation.

outline.heading: How small we are in the cosmos
outline.gist: Among a hundred billion galaxies we are an untraceable speck; what we can observe is tiny beside what Allah created.

outline.heading: Humbled that Allah cares for us
outline.gist: Despite our smallness Allah gives us attention and sees potential in us, which should humble us.

outline.heading: Recap of the detained and recitation
outline.gist: Those detained at the Judgment are asked why they no longer support one another; they have submitted, but too late.

outline.heading: 'You came at us from the right'
outline.gist: Followers accuse leaders of coming with power and authority, or with a show of piety, to mislead them.

outline.heading: The leaders' reply: you were never believers
outline.gist: We had no sultan over you, neither compelling argument nor power; you were already transgressors.

outline.heading: Echo chambers are older than algorithms
outline.gist: People always surrounded themselves with those who repeat their views; technology just does it more efficiently, and both bad and good feeds are open for business.

outline.heading: Leaders and followers are both accountable
outline.gist: Followers hope to argue their way out by blaming leaders, but each is accountable, and leaders also carry those who followed them.

outline.heading: Beware of hearing only what you want
outline.gist: Growth comes from voices that make you uncomfortable and make you revise your choices.

outline.heading: A teacher's job is to challenge, not mirror
outline.gist: A lesson is not a call-in radio show; if you leave without questioning yourself, the teacher has failed.

outline.heading: Leaders as the mirror of public desires
outline.gist: A shameless, lying leader of the strongest country stands because people want to hear him, the reverse of a leader's duty and a sign of the end of time.

outline.heading: The word of our Lord has come true
outline.gist: Allah's word that Hell will be filled with transgressors applies to both leader and follower.

outline.heading: Ghawayah: misguided while thinking you are guided
outline.gist: Ghawayah differs from dalal: it is walking the wrong path believing it right, which is why Muslims question themselves.

outline.heading: Partners in punishment
outline.gist: Allah comments on the exchange: both groups share the punishment.

outline.heading: Criminals against Allah's law
outline.gist: Mujrim in the Quran means one who breaks Allah's law and does not repent, not a breaker of national law.

outline.heading: La ilaha illa Allah, rejected by arrogance
outline.gist: One of two places the full phrase appears; it is the best thing the prophets said and renews iman, and only arrogance can reject it.

outline.heading: The simplest and most liberating truth
outline.gist: One source behind all existence is the most obvious explanation; it frees a person from fear of anyone, so free will is offered to Allah alone.

outline.heading: Humanity has worshipped everything
outline.gist: Idols have been animals, plants, rocks, stars and more; none of it worked.

outline.heading: Worshipping people under another name
outline.gist: Kings once claimed divine lineage; the Quran ended that language, but people still obey rulers unconditionally.

outline.heading: Neither poet nor madman: the same truth as all prophets
outline.gist: Bal refutes them: he brought the truth and confirmed the message of every earlier messenger.

outline.heading: Repaid only for what you did
outline.gist: The tone hardens after their insult to the Prophet; compensation matches deeds exactly.

outline.heading: The exception: the sincere servants
outline.gist: The rule of exact repayment has an exception found across the Quran.

outline.heading: Sincerity is granted, not achieved
outline.gist: Mukhlas means one whom Allah has made sincere; we strive, but Allah bestows it.

outline.heading: Rewarded far beyond deeds
outline.gist: No deed could earn Allah's reward; seeing sincere effort, He opens the gates of His generosity.

outline.heading: Known provision, food of pleasure, couches facing one another
outline.gist: Fawakih means food eaten for enjoyment, not hunger; they are honoured and enjoy the company of those they love.

outline.heading: A pure drink without intoxication
outline.gist: The drink brings joy without harming body or mind; sobriety is the gift that makes us human.

outline.heading: Loyal spouses like protected pearls
outline.gist: Spouses with eyes for no one else, beautiful as guarded pearls.

outline.heading: Every kind of joy, none of it harmful
outline.gist: Food, drink, company, honour and setting are all covered, and unlike worldly pleasure there is no price to pay later.

outline.heading: The people of Paradise also turn to one another
outline.gist: Mirroring verse 27, the believers too question each other, leading into the next session.

MV-eErTg80k.title: Tazkiyah Pearls 9: Values and Tawbah
MV-eErTg80k.one_line: Why habitual sin reveals what we truly believe, how principles become values, and why real tawbah needs genuine remorse and a plan.
MV-eErTg80k.summary: He first closes the topic of humbleness: it is simply recognising our reality as servants, so self-proclaimed or artificial humility is a form of arrogance, and without humbleness nobody can learn. He then lays out four levels: a principle from the Quran makes a value valid, a value is the deep definition you carry, an ethic is how it shows up in a given situation, and behaviour is the lifelong practice. The core problem is the gap between what we say we believe and what we actually believe. Using lowering the gaze as an example for men, he argues that a sin repeated constantly is not weakness but a hidden belief that it is not really wrong, buried in an inner black box nobody wants to open. Some go further and bend the religion to match their habits. Values must be consistent, not conditional, which is the steep path of the Quran. Tazkiyah, technically, is turning Quranic principles into values. He then teaches tawbah as the clearest window into values: it needs remorse, stopping now, and a plan. Remorse is impossible if you never believed the act was wrong, and nostalgia for past sins shows tawbah has not happened. A plan removes the cause each time, so tawbah from one sin gradually cleans out many. He ends by urging deep reflection to define values with their real exceptions.

outline.heading: Humbleness is the servant's reality; artificial humility is arrogance
outline.gist: Allah's essence is greatness; ours is servitude, so humbleness is just honesty about what we are. Declaring your own humility reveals arrogance.

outline.heading: Seeking strength and status through Allah
outline.gist: Wanting integrity and status is fine, but they must be sought from Allah who owns them and grants them lastingly.

outline.heading: Be the humble company you enjoy
outline.gist: Humble people are easy to be around because they do not compare or point out flaws; become that person.

outline.heading: Without humbleness you cannot learn
outline.gist: Learning requires admitting ignorance; the humble learn from anyone, of any age or background, and learn fastest.

outline.heading: Serve even before you understand
outline.gist: Service manifests humbleness and can make up for a lack of clarity on the concepts.

outline.heading: Principle, value, ethic and behaviour
outline.gist: The principle validates a value; the value is honesty defined in depth; using honesty as the example.

outline.heading: Ethics shift with the situation; the Quran supplies principles
outline.gist: The definition of honesty stays fixed while its expression changes by question and setting; principles are already set by the Quran.

outline.heading: What you claim to believe versus what you really believe
outline.gist: Beliefs float in the psyche as nice ideas until they are captured and made second nature, which takes time.

outline.heading: The bedouins told to say 'we submitted'
outline.gist: Allah corrected their claim of full faith, showing a transitional period before belief enters the heart.

outline.heading: Lowering the gaze: habitual sin is not weakness
outline.gist: Everyone says looking is forbidden, yet most do it constantly; frequent sin shows a gap between claimed and real belief.

outline.heading: The black box of real values
outline.gist: Most never open the sealed box inside; doing so reveals a long scroll of excuses that is the true belief.

outline.heading: Bending the religion to fit our habits
outline.gist: Some, rather than change, reinterpret Allah's words to match their values, producing a morphed Islam rooted in arrogance and fear of change.

outline.heading: Values are consistent, not conditional
outline.gist: Generosity only when wealthy or in a good mood is a preference, not a value.

outline.heading: The steep path: giving when you are also in need
outline.gist: Freeing a slave or feeding the hungry on a day of hunger is the obstacle that proves an ethic is unconditional.

outline.heading: Tazkiyah defined: turning Quranic principles into values
outline.gist: Once values are correctly coded, ongoing coaching is unnecessary; failure to practise usually means you do not really accept the ruling.

outline.heading: Do we truly believe in accountability?
outline.gist: Extended to resurrection and judgment, the same gap explains the state of the ummah; facing real beliefs is frightening but the first step.

outline.heading: Tawbah: the door that never closes
outline.gist: The Prophet repented a hundred times a day; the door stays open until the sun rises from the west or death arrives.

outline.heading: The elements of tawbah
outline.gist: Remorse for the past, stopping the sin now, and a plan for the future, plus restitution where rights were taken.

outline.heading: Remorse requires believing the act was wrong
outline.gist: Regret is the core of tawbah, and you cannot regret what you never thought was wrong.

outline.heading: Outgrowing a sin or missing it is not tawbah
outline.gist: Stopping because of age, sickness or lack of time, or looking back fondly on those days, means tawbah has not happened.

outline.heading: Using Allah's principles to feel superior
outline.gist: Saying a lifestyle is forbidden because it feels good to say, while craving it inside, is another kind of arrogance.

outline.heading: Why men fall: an unconvinced value meets opportunity
outline.gist: Craving the forbidden comes from not being convinced it should be forbidden; when power and status arrive later in life, the hidden belief surfaces.

outline.heading: Expose your values before time exposes them
outline.gist: Allah conceals your true beliefs; it is your job to uncover and change them, reaching genuine regret.

outline.heading: The plan: find and remove the culprit
outline.gist: Ask why you sinned: a value, environment, friends, timing, routine. Intention alone with nothing changed guarantees a relapse.

outline.heading: Tawbah from one sin becomes tawbah from all
outline.gist: Each relapse reveals another cause to remove; since sins feed one another, clearing influences removes sins you no longer notice.

outline.heading: Building a value through reflection
outline.gist: Contemplate a value like honesty in depth, knowing its genuine exceptions so you do not invent new ones.

MgGICXQfErI.title: Tazkiyah Pearls 7: Humbleness, Part 1 (Vanity)
MgGICXQfErI.one_line: Humbleness as the master ethic: vanity as entitlement and expectation, its antidote in praising Allah, and Qarun as the Quran's example.
MgGICXQfErI.summary: Returning to the pendulum of self-value, he says the nafs keeps reattaching sources of worth, so vigilance is lifelong. Humbleness, the sum of confidence and humility, is the master of all ethics and is traditionally taught first, since other lessons can harm someone who lacks it. This session covers the first level, confidence versus vanity. Vanity rests on entitlement and expectation: claiming achievements as one's own and deciding what one's effort is worth, a judgment that belongs to Allah alone. Even an agnostic must admit that parents, teachers and circumstances made every success possible, and no one enters Paradise by deeds. We are already in infinite debt to Allah, so expecting an easy life for becoming religious is vanity. Confidence is trust in the potential and story Allah gave you. The antidote is hamd: turning the spotlight from oneself to Allah, knowing that even the ability to thank Him is a blessing. Qarun, who claimed his wealth came from his own knowledge, was swallowed by the earth. He adds that emotions produced by the pendulum's swings are not genuine, which is why people struggle to feel real love or sadness. Apply this only to yourself, never let praise fool you about yourself, and meet success with praise and istighfar as in Surah An-Nasr.

outline.heading: The pendulum always swings a little
outline.gist: Even after cutting false sources of worth, the nafs keeps forming new connections that swing self-value.

outline.heading: Humbleness is taught first
outline.gist: Vigilance is part of being alive; humbleness is usually taught for months before anything else because other lessons can harm someone who lacks it.

outline.heading: Confidence plus humility: the master of all ethics
outline.gist: The first level balances vanity and low self-esteem with confidence, the second balances arrogance and inferiority with humility; together they make humbleness, which generates every other ethic.

outline.heading: Vanity: entitlement and expectation
outline.gist: Vanity claims achievements and the praise they deserve, and expects returns from Allah; deciding what your effort is worth takes Allah's role.

outline.heading: You are the sum of others' efforts
outline.gist: Even without belief in God, parents, mentors, teachers and experiences made your success possible, so taking full credit is false.

outline.heading: Only Allah decides what your effort is worth
outline.gist: Naming any percentage of credit is vanity; aim for Allah to give you something for your effort, since no one enters Paradise by deeds but by His mercy.

outline.heading: Rephrasing success: Allah allowed it
outline.gist: A million things could have gone wrong, yet Allah protected every step despite your shortcomings.

outline.heading: The Prophet enters Makkah with his head bowed
outline.gist: At his moment of triumph his forehead touched his mount; since body and spirit belong to Allah, credit belongs to the Owner.

outline.heading: We deserve nothing: we are in debt
outline.gist: Entitlement and high expectations for oneself create the big ego; asking for more while owing Allah everything is laughable.

outline.heading: Expecting a red carpet for becoming religious
outline.gist: Believing that turning to Allah should bring an easy life is vanity and leads to disappointment.

outline.heading: Confidence versus low self-esteem
outline.gist: Confidence trusts the potential and story Allah gave you; low self-esteem believes Allah sees nothing good in you.

outline.heading: The four main diseases of the heart
outline.gist: Vanity, arrogance, envy and ostentation; the first two are direct opposites of humbleness.

outline.heading: The antidote: hamd turns the spotlight to the sky
outline.gist: Saying all praise belongs to Allah redirects praise from yourself to the One who deserves it.

outline.heading: Confidence is hoping Allah will praise you
outline.gist: Keep giving full effort hoping He praises you; when interviewed about your success, credit Allah's family, challenges and mentors and feel shy of claiming your small part.

outline.heading: Thanking Allah is itself a blessing
outline.gist: A prophet asked how to thank Allah when thanking is a blessing too, and was told that now he truly thanked; praise has no end, as blessings cannot be counted.

outline.heading: Qarun: success goes to his head
outline.gist: Once a follower of Musa, he grew so rich that even his keys needed strong men to carry; his people warned him not to exult.

outline.heading: Emotions from the pendulum are not genuine
outline.gist: Vain joy is masked happiness; living with a swinging pendulum dulls us to real love, empathy and even sadness at verses about death and Hell.

outline.heading: Raw emotion and righteous anger
outline.gist: Anger from feeling inferior is toxic and harmful, while anger at injustice or the breaking of Allah's word is genuine and not violent.

outline.heading: Qarun's reply and his end
outline.gist: Musa sent others to advise him; he claimed his wealth came from his own knowledge and work, and the earth swallowed him and his wealth.

outline.heading: Seeing one's own position as a blessing
outline.gist: He sees his role of serving as Allah's gift he does not deserve, which Allah could give to someone better if he stopped seeing it so.

outline.heading: Do not apply this to others
outline.gist: Belittling someone else's effort or diplomas is as wrong as inflating your own; assume they deserve much praise.

outline.heading: Never let anyone fool you about you
outline.gist: Accept praise as kindness but do not believe it, as Qarun and all vain people did; whatever is good is from Allah and the mistakes are yours.

outline.heading: Confidence without claiming credit
outline.gist: See potential, decree and Allah's love when you look in the mirror, while saying alhamdulillah for every achievement and seeking forgiveness for what you did poorly.

outline.heading: Praise and istighfar at the moment of victory
outline.gist: Entering Makkah, the Prophet was told to glorify, praise and seek forgiveness; focus on where you fell short on the way to success.

outline.heading: Outro

rfhXS8QOWYs.title: Ramadan Reminders 1446: Part 2, Badr and Doing What Is Right
rfhXS8QOWYs.one_line: At mid-Ramadan, push through the fatigue, and learn from Badr that open oppression must be answered and truth outweighs every interest.
rfhXS8QOWYs.summary: On the fourteenth of Ramadan, the sheikh reminds listeners that half the month remains and even a sincere final minute can outweigh what others gained all month, so this is the time for repentance and hard questions about one's relationship with Allah. Ramadan is a marathon; the nafs waits until you are tired, then argues you out of Fajr and taraweeh, but growth lies in the last push, so renew your intention. Having worked on less food for two weeks, you have proven you can do more with less, which shows how far needs differ from wants. Ramadan, though, is about what is right. That leads to Badr on 17 Ramadan 2 AH, in the first Ramadan Muslims ever fasted. Comfortable in Medina, some companions resisted going after the caravan carrying their stolen wealth, but the issue was haqq, not money. Openly seized rights, as in Palestine, are not yours to forgive; take them back, then forgive on your own terms. Al-Anfal recounts the reluctance, the promise of one of two outcomes and how each army saw the other as small. In the second khutbah he praises the discipline of the 314, tells of the two boys who killed Abu Jahl, and notes that Abu Jahl died more committed to falsehood than many Muslims are to truth.

outline.heading: Opening
Half the month is left
outline.gist: Tonight marks the middle of Ramadan. Its baraka is such that one sincere final minute can bring what others missed all month, so fourteen wasted days still leave fifteen.

outline.heading: The month of repentance: ask the hard questions
outline.gist: A scholar he cites knew of no repentance reaching its full potential outside Ramadan. Ask yourself how you are doing with Allah, how far down the path you are, and how closely you follow the Prophet.

outline.heading: Never lose hope, even with a day left
outline.gist: If you dislike the answers, that is good news: Allah accepts repentance now and gives the inner strength to turn things around. Even on the last Friday, with a day or two left, effort can achieve what others did not.

outline.heading: It costs only a little more heart
outline.gist: Paradise is open, Hell closed, and Allah calls the lost back to Him. It takes only contemplation, sincerity, standing a little longer and a prostration with more heart in it.

outline.heading: The blessing of all blessings
outline.gist: Once you find it you will never give it up; all the world's riches do not equal it. If you have not found it, keep knocking. Ramadan is a marathon, and Allah looks for grit.

outline.heading: The nafs negotiates when you are tired
outline.gist: Dehydrated and tired mid-month, you start bargaining over Fajr at the masjid and skipping taraweeh because it is only sunnah. The ego fights unfairly, waiting until you are weak.

outline.heading: Growth is in the last push
outline.gist: When you cannot go further but go one more mile, you find your real strength and find Allah. If it were easy everyone would do it; what you ask for is expensive.

outline.heading: Resurface your intention
outline.gist: Allah's commodity is Paradise. Dig the intention you began with out from under the clutter of fatigue, hunger and busyness; you have not reached your goal yet.

outline.heading: The fatigue fades, the regret stays
outline.gist: Ramadan is a few days and will end (2:184). Two days of rest erase the tiredness; what remains is either reward or regret at not having applied yourself.

outline.heading: Not can you, but will you do more with less
outline.gist: Nobody looked forward to work without coffee or school without lunch, yet after fourteen days it is normal. You proved you can do the same job with less sustenance.

outline.heading: What you need versus what you want
outline.gist: When food returns, productivity should rise 20 to 30 percent. Allah shows you need far less than you think; the ego wants everything for itself, and its greed has no end.

outline.heading: Ramadan is about what is right
outline.gist: Ramadan is about neither wants nor needs but what is right. That leads to Badr: 17 Ramadan 2 AH, 1444 lunar years ago, in the first Ramadan Muslims ever fasted.

outline.heading: Go take back what they stole
outline.gist: Desert Arabs had no habit of fasting, yet seventeen days in, the Prophet called them out to Abu Sufyan's caravan carrying their openly stolen wealth. He will teach Badr every Ramadan.

outline.heading: Comfortable believers who disliked the pursuit (8:5)
outline.gist: Two years after the Hijra they were settled, at peace, with the Prophet teaching among them, and had forgotten the stolen wealth. Why poke the bear, they asked, when you taught us wealth does not matter?

outline.heading: Rights openly taken are not yours to forgive
outline.gist: Not daily slights but rights seized openly and never acknowledged, as in Palestine. Forgiving that is weakness and even sinful; take back what is yours, then give it back on your terms, not the oppressor's.

outline.heading: Arguing about the truth after it was clear (8:6)
outline.gist: A Muslim's integrity does not let him give up his right. Some believers argued, frightened, as if being marched to their graves.

outline.heading: Truth outweighs every interest
outline.gist: You do not argue with the right thing; you do it. Truth is the heaviest weight in any decision, above your own or your family's interest. Allah promised one of two outcomes (8:7).

outline.heading: Allah willed the truth established
outline.gist: Most hoped for the caravan, but Allah wanted truth established and falsehood exposed, using the word truth six times in a few verses. The 314 set out, the caravan slipped toward the coast, and Quraysh marched a thousand men.

outline.heading: Three hundred horsemen against two
outline.gist: At Badr a small band stood with the Prophet against a power no one had beaten in decades; Quraysh had more cavalry than the Muslims had soldiers.

outline.heading: The Prophet's dream: they seemed few (8:43-44)
outline.gist: Expecting a slaughter, the companions were afraid until the Prophet told them he had seen the enemy as few. Facing off, the Muslims saw Quraysh as fewer than they were and grew calm.

outline.heading: The day of distinction
outline.gist: Quraysh also saw the Muslims as few and dropped their guard. Allah decreed a day separating truth from falsehood that would never be forgotten; fasting, they won the victory without which most in the room would not be Muslim.

outline.heading: Interlude
Ramadan teaches discipline
outline.gist: The 314 had the inner discipline to march while fasting against an enemy they could not imagine beating. An ummah without self-discipline goes nowhere; each person must hold himself, not others, in check.

outline.heading: Two boys looking for Abu Jahl
outline.gist: Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, worried by the odds, felt a tug on each side: two young men asking which one was Abu Jahl, one sent by his mother, the other because he had abused the Prophet. They ran in like arrows and brought him down.

outline.heading: Ibn Mas'ud on Abu Jahl's chest
outline.gist: Both boys claimed the killing blow and the Prophet credited both. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, a small man, then stood on the dying Abu Jahl's chest, and Abu Jahl mocked him as a little shepherd.

outline.heading: Who won today? A man who knew the truth
outline.gist: Dying, Abu Jahl asked who had won, still committed to his cause. He had admitted that Muhammad was truthful but refused to follow him because his clan had no prophet to match.

outline.heading: More committed to falsehood than we are to truth
outline.gist: It is close to pathetic that a man who knew he was wrong was more committed than Muslims who stand for the rights of the oppressed. Ramadan reminds us to put food and distraction aside for what is right.

outline.heading: Outro

45:23.en: Have you seen he who has taken as his god his [own] desire, and Allah has sent him astray due to knowledge and has set a seal upon his hearing and his heart and put over his vision a veil? So who will guide him after Allah? Then will you not be reminded

WyjxQZBddbQ.title: Tazkiyah Pearls 10: Principles and Tools of Tazkiyah
WyjxQZBddbQ.one_line: A reference session on the four principles of striving against the self and the external, internal, lifestyle and reinforcement methods of tazkiyah.
WyjxQZBddbQ.summary: He frames the session as a reference to revisit. Starting from the Prophet's fear that his ummah would obey greed, follow desire and admire their own opinions, he explains the verse about taking one's desire as a god, and draws a second reading: people can reshape their very image of Allah to suit what they want. Striving against the self rests on four principles. Change must be gradual and gentle, because the self adapts but can break, and overnight transformations rebound. You need raw honesty with yourself and Allah even while keeping a social face, since nothing can be treated in denial. Small habits must be completely consistent, as Ali kept his bedtime dhikr even on a night of battle. And a sin must be left completely, with something good substituted to fill the gap. He then groups the methods. External: knowledge to feed new thoughts into the cycle of thought, feeling and action; good companions; mentors who teach by how they live; and a supportive environment. Internal: contemplation and exercises such as doing a disliked act of service daily until the self stops resisting. Lifestyle: sleep on the Prophet's pattern, not filling the stomach, a steady routine and physical health. Reinforcement: dhikr, dua and the Quran. He asks listeners to take what benefits them and apply it.

outline.heading: A reference session on the basics of tazkiyah
outline.gist: The material is dense and meant to be revisited; he is summarising a third of Islam in a short series.

outline.heading: What the Prophet feared most for his ummah
outline.gist: Obeyed greed, followed desire and vanity in one's own opinion, all diseases of the inner self.

outline.heading: Taking one's desire as a god
outline.gist: The self rarely wants anything for a good reason, so some scholars had beginners simply oppose their desires for years.

outline.heading: Shaping Allah to fit our desires
outline.gist: The verse also warns of distorting one's image of Allah; the angry want a god of wrath, the weak a god of endless mercy, but He is who He is.

outline.heading: Striving against the self: principles and methods
outline.gist: The self thinks it knows what is best but does not; he will give four principles and four methods of striving.

outline.heading: Principle one: gradual and gentle change
outline.gist: The self is remarkably adaptable, but flexibility does not mean it cannot be broken by trauma.

outline.heading: Harshness breaks the self, as with children
outline.gist: Treating children too harshly can cause lifelong damage; the aim of tazkiyah is to reshape the self, not destroy it.

outline.heading: Why overnight transformations rebound
outline.gist: Someone who goes from no prayer to every sunnah at once usually collapses; extreme change needs extreme circumstances.

outline.heading: Principle two: honesty and self-transparency
outline.gist: If you rationalise your habits or think yourself better than you are, nothing changes; some scholars put this first.

outline.heading: A social mask for people, raw honesty before Allah
outline.gist: Concealing sins from others is right, but you must face yourself without the persona; like a patient in denial, you cannot be treated otherwise.

outline.heading: Closing the door on the messy room
outline.gist: People avoid looking inside because the mess feels overwhelming, then deny how far behind they are.

outline.heading: Principle three: small, consistent habits
outline.gist: The deeds most beloved to Allah are consistent even if small, such as daily dhikr and a little Quran.

outline.heading: Ali's bedtime dhikr, even on the night of battle
outline.gist: Taught the bedtime tasbih by the Prophet, Ali never missed it, in any condition.

outline.heading: Making daily reflection a fixed habit
outline.gist: Habits you add, like ten to fifteen minutes of deep thought each day, must be self-driven and constant.

outline.heading: Principle four: complete abstinence
outline.gist: As in recovery from alcohol, leaving a sin means cutting off everything associated with it.

outline.heading: Substitution fills the gap
outline.gist: Leaving a habit leaves a void; without something fulfilling in its place you rebound, as many do after Ramadan.

outline.heading: The principles recapped: treat the self like a child
outline.gist: Gentleness, honest courage that also breeds humbleness, resetting broken habits, and stopping cold turkey except for addictions needing supervision.

outline.heading: Four categories of method and the cycle of thought, feeling and action
outline.gist: Negative feelings, thoughts and deeds feed each other in a vicious cycle that an outside force can break.

outline.heading: External method: knowledge
outline.gist: New information gives contemplation fresh material and turns the cycle virtuous; inner effort fails without outside teaching.

outline.heading: External method: companionship
outline.gist: Your time and attention are your most valuable assets; bad friends undo everything at any age, so keep company that draws you closer to Allah.

outline.heading: External method: mentorship
outline.gist: The path is walked with someone who has walked it; Allah sent a Prophet with the Book, beginning a chain of teachers.

outline.heading: A week with a teacher who barely ate or slept
outline.gist: He recalls struggling to keep up with a late teacher; observing such a life stays with you.

outline.heading: External method: environment
outline.gist: Where you spend your time shapes you, in religion and in any craft, such as becoming a good doctor.

outline.heading: Internal method: contemplation
outline.gist: Deep thought on important topics changes how you feel and act.

outline.heading: Internal method: exercises against the self
outline.gist: Do a disliked act of service every day until the self stops resisting, so you learn to recognise its pushback.

outline.heading: Lifestyle: sleep on the Prophet's pattern
outline.gist: Tazkiyah fails without good sleep; the Prophet slept early, rose for prayer and napped by day, as did his own teachers.

outline.heading: Resetting the routine: camps near Damascus and army service
outline.gist: Summer tazkiyah camps without electricity, and compulsory army service at university, reset his broken routine; camping can do the same for families.

outline.heading: Lifestyle: never filling the stomach
outline.gist: Muslims follow everything except the hadith on thirds of the stomach; healthy eating is part of the path.

outline.heading: Lifestyle: a steady daily routine
outline.gist: Structure is healthy, not boring; psychiatrists prescribe routine against depression.

outline.heading: Lifestyle: physical health and the heart
outline.gist: Spiritual terms are named after body parts for a reason; a neglected body will not carry a healthy spiritual heart.

outline.heading: Reinforcement: dhikr, dua and Quran
outline.gist: Specific words of remembrance counter vanity and arrogance; reciting Quran, hadith and stories reinforces every concept.
